front: What are the three places to look for help on a Linux system, from quickest to deepest?
back: `command --help` for a usage summary, `man command` for the full manual page, and `/usr/share/doc/` for README files, change logs and examples.

front: How do you search inside a man page, go to the next match and quit?
back: Type `/word` and Enter to search, `n` for the next match (`N` for the previous) and `q` to quit. Space or `f` is the next page and `b` the previous.

front: Name the man page sections NAME, SYNOPSIS and DESCRIPTION: what does each hold?
back: NAME: the command and a one-line description. SYNOPSIS: how to call it. DESCRIPTION: what it does, with every option.

front: In `cp [OPTION]... SOURCE DEST`, what do the square brackets, the dots and the capital letters mean?
back: Square brackets: optional. Three dots: can be repeated. Capital letters: a placeholder you replace with a real name, such as a file.

front: What do manual sections 1, 5 and 8 hold?
back: 1: user commands and programs. 5: file formats and configuration files such as `/etc/passwd`. 8: system administration commands, usually for root.

front: `passwd` is both a command and a file format. How do you open the page about the file?
back: `man 5 passwd`. Plain `man passwd` shows the first page it finds, section 1 (the command). The header shows the section, like `PASSWD(5)`.

front: Mira doesn’t know which command changes passwords. How can she search the one-line descriptions?
back: `man -k WORD` or `apropos WORD`, which search by keyword.

front: What do `man -f NAME` and `whatis NAME` do?
back: They list the short description of exactly that name, in every section where it exists.

front: What does `man -w 5 passwd` print, and where do man pages live?
back: The path of the page file: `/usr/share/man/man5/passwd.5.gz`. Pages live under `/usr/share/man/`, one folder per section, compressed with gzip.

front: What are the two usual ways to get a quick usage summary from a command?
back: `--help` (long form) and `-h` (short form). Many programs support both, some only one. The output starts with a `Usage:` line.

front: Why is `-h` not always the way to ask for help?
back: In `ls -lh` and `df -h` it means human-readable sizes. `--help` is the safe choice, and `--version` prints the version.

front: Why does `man cd` not give a page of its own, and what do you use instead?
back: `cd` is a Bash builtin, part of the shell. Use the builtin `help`, for example `help cd`.

front: `cp --help` scrolls past too fast. What can Mira do?
back: Pipe it: `cp --help | head -n 3` shows the start, `cp --help | less` lets her scroll.

front: What does `/usr/share/doc/` contain?
back: One directory per package, named after it, with README files, licence texts (`copyright`), change logs (`changelog.gz`) and often an `examples` folder.

front: How can you read a documentation file ending in `.gz`?
back: With `zcat` (print a gzip file) or `zless`, for example `zcat /usr/share/doc/bash/README.gz | head -n 3`.

front: What is an info page and which command reads it?
back: Documentation, especially for GNU tools, organised as nodes with links between them. You read it with `info`, for example `info coreutils`.

front: Which keys move around in `info`, and how do you leave?
back: `n`, `p` and `u` go to the next, previous and parent node, Enter follows a link, `/` searches and `q` quits.

front: How does `locate` find files, and what is its drawback?
back: It searches a database of file names, rebuilt regularly (usually daily), so it is instant. It doesn’t know files created since the last update and still lists deleted ones.

front: What does `updatedb` do, and who can run it?
back: It rebuilds the database that `locate` searches, and it needs root.

front: When should Mira use `find` instead of `locate`?
back: When she needs a current result: `find` searches the real disk, which is slower but always up to date.
